title: The Hook and the Horizon
subtitle: The Shore I Choose · Chapter 2 of 10
content:
The Lanternweald was apparently a place that had been built by people who couldn't agree on which century they lived in.

Its paths wound through old stone houses, tiled roofs, little gardens, and bridges that crossed streams too shallow to justify the engineering. A spring beneath a ring of lanterns occupied the center of the settlement. Someone had left bread on a bench and written a note asking whoever took the last piece to make more.

Maui called the square Lanternwell.

“Who lives here?” I asked.

“People who found it. People who needed it. People who haven't decided. I haven't taken a census.”

“You could.”

“I could do a lot of things. Most of them involve a hook.”

He took me to Tideglass Cove, where he had left the canoe. The water there was calmer than on the outer beach, sheltered by two headlands shaped like open hands. A half-finished dock leaned into the tide.

“You know boats?” he asked.

“I don't know.”

“Great. You can discover whether you hate them before I let you near the sail.”

Before he let me touch the rigging, Maui made me walk the length of the dock with him. The planks had been patched in three colors. One rocked beneath my foot.

"That's not safe," I said.

"You're learning very quickly."

"You're not going to repair it?"

"I didn't build it. I don't know which boards the tide undermines. There's a difference between fixing something and making it look fixed."

That surprised me. "You know the difference?"

His tattooed miniature folded its arms.

"I am a man of infinite hidden talents."

We found Fen beside the small tide board, measuring the water against a painted notch. They were older than I expected, their hands knotted from years of rope and salt.

"The west edge is closed," Fen told us. "It needs a proper support, not another hero pretending a loose plank is charming."

Maui sighed. "I get this speech every time."

"Then it should be familiar."

Fen directed us to the sounder landing instead and asked whether we wanted a short lesson in knots used for temporary mooring. The first knot was a bowline. The second was a warning about knots tied in wet line: they could look neat and still slip as the rope dried.

I tried to copy their hands. My first loop collapsed. My second held until I pulled it from the wrong direction.

Maui started to help without asking. He stopped himself, mid-reach.

"Would you like me to show you?"

"Yes. Slowly."

He demonstrated. I watched his fingers more closely than his smile. The movements looked familiar, yet when I tried them my hands shook.

"I should know this," I muttered.

"Should you?"

"I don't know. It feels like I've done it before."

Fen passed me another length of line. "Then you'll either remember or learn it again. Nobody's giving marks."

The third attempt held. I looked up, breathless, and Maui's triumphant grin softened when he saw how relieved I was.

"Good," he said simply.

Fen made me check it twice before they would call it good. I was glad of that, too.

Later, when we stepped into the canoe, I noticed a small carved wooden fish tied above the bow. Its tail had broken and been repaired with darker wood.

"What's that?"

"An old traveling charm," Maui said. "Not mine. Somebody left it here after borrowing the boat, and I kept it. The fellow who made it was very proud of his fish."

"Does it work?"

"Depends what you need a fish to do."

I laughed. He adjusted the sail with one hand and pointed toward the headlands.

"That opening is the safe return course. If the wind shifts, we come back. You don't have to prove anything by staying out."

I wanted to tell him I didn't need a warning. Instead I asked him to repeat it, and he did without making me feel small.

By noon I had learned that knots obeyed rules, my fingers remembered more than my head did, and Maui believed every mistake was improved by an audience. He demonstrated a bowline with extravagant confidence. I repeated it incorrectly. He made a speech about the importance of watching legends carefully.

Then he inspected my second attempt and went quiet.

“That's good,” he admitted.

I looked down. The knot lay neat and sturdy in my palms.

“I didn't remember learning.”

“You still learned.”

It was such a simple distinction that I nearly missed it.

Later we pushed off from the cove. Maui kept the canoe close to shore and explained how the wind moved across the sail. He spoke of stars as navigational companions, but admitted the sky above the Lanternweald did not always obey the ones he knew. I asked him whether that frightened him.

“Frightened? Me?”

The little tattoo of Maui on his chest covered its eyes.

“Okay, challenged,” he amended. “There's a difference.”

The wind rose. I pulled the wrong line and the sail snapped, making the whole craft lean.

“Release it,” Maui said.

I froze.

“Hey. Look at me. Not the water. The line.”

My hands loosened. The sail settled. We righted ourselves.

On shore I expected a lecture. Instead Maui gave me a cup of fresh water and sat beside the overturned canoe, watching the light.

“Why didn't you just fix it?” I asked.

“Because you wanted to learn.”

“You could have been hurt.”

He shrugged, then saw my expression and corrected himself. “I knew where the safe shore was. I wouldn't have made you carry the risk alone.”

The thought sat somewhere deep inside me: somebody had once confused teaching me with leaving me responsible for everything. I could feel the shape of the memory without seeing its face.

Maui watched me with an unusual stillness.

“Did something come back?”

“Only a feeling.”

“Good one?”

“No.”

He didn't demand the story. He tossed a small piece of driftwood between his hands.

“I've had whole islands call me a hero and still not believe I belonged there,” he said. “A feeling can stick around longer than a fact. Doesn't mean it gets to captain the boat.”

I laughed, despite myself. “You turn everything into a boat lesson?”

“Only the important stuff.”

On the way back we passed Fen carrying a shallow basket of shellfish. They paused to ask how the lesson went.

"I only nearly overturned the canoe once," I said.

"Then it's too early to trust you with the north channel."

Maui made a wounded noise.

"That was my very careful instruction."

"Then you need better instructions," Fen answered.

They showed us the tide marks beside the landing. The water was already falling, and the shallow sandbar would be exposed before the evening. The lesson hadn't ended when we stepped out of the boat; someone needed to know how to bring it home without scraping the hull.

I drew the safe route in my notebook. Fen corrected the bend around the western post. Maui carried the boat up the sounder ramp rather than lifting it over the damaged rail.

It was a small thing, but it made the cove feel inhabited by people who would remember whether we had left the mooring safe.

"Tomorrow, if you're willing," I told Fen, "I'd like to learn the tide board."

"Ask me after breakfast," they said. "I have a living to make first."

When we returned to Lanternwell, I tied the canoe with the knot I had learned. Maui tested it once, then left it alone.

The rope held.

For the first time since waking on the shore, I allowed myself to believe that I might, too.
